_comment: DBE NSC Grade 12 Geography P2, November 2025. Full-fidelity transcription:
every sub-question verbatim from the question paper (text layer read
page-by-page with pdftotext -layout, figures verified against rendered
page images), memo answers verbatim from the official Marking Guidelines.
Figures are described in [FIGURE: ...] brackets inside 'context'.
FORMAT (same as 2024): P2 is Rural and Urban Settlements (Q1), Economic
Geography of South Africa (Q2) plus Section B mapwork (Q3, 1:50 000
topographical map 2529CC eMALAHLENI (WITBANK) and 1:10 000 orthophoto map
2529 CC 15 eMALAHLENI (WITBANK)).
The physical map sheets are separate and not in this repo, so map-read
inputs for calculations come from the memo's accepted values.
MEMO ANOMALY (same as 2024): page 3 of the marking-guidelines PDF is a
marking-principles demonstration (a sample marked script from a different
paper - e.g. it shows '1.1.1 A (South Atlantic High)'). It is NOT the
answer key for this paper; the real answers start on memo page 4
('SECTION A'). The memo's final line misprints 'TOTAL SECTION B: 150'
where it means GRAND TOTAL: 150.
Download URLs: the 2025 November papers were sourced as local PDFs; the
DBE fileticket download URLs were not captured, so paper_download_url and
memo_download_url are null.

questions.context: 1.3 Refer to the graph below showing the percentage of rural population in South Africa from 2017 to 2024 and the extract on land restitution. [FIGURE (adapted from https://www.theglobaleconomy.com/South-Africa/rural_population_percent): Bar graph 'PERCENTAGE OF RURAL POPULATION IN SOUTH AFRICA' with values 2017: 34,66; 2018: 34,16; 2019: 33,65; 2020: 33,14; 2021: 32,65; 2022: 32,15; 2023: 31,67; 2024: 31,18.] EXTRACT - MOLETELE CITRUS FRUIT FARM SHOWCASING THE SUCCESS OF A LAND RESTITUTION PROGRAMME IN LIMPOPO: 'The Moletele community opted to take their land back and this has resulted in a successful land restitution programme. The newest agricultural technology and rows of well-maintained citrus trees at Moletele Farm in Hoedspruit are clear indicators of this success. The lime-producing farm in Hoedspruit is a joint venture project of the Moletele communal property association (holding a 51% stake) and the established commercial fruit producer Komati Fruit Group. A total of 30 permanent and 60 temporary jobs have already been created. The programme transfers skills to the workforce and community. Proceeds are given to thousands of families in the Moletele community. A bursary scheme makes it possible for profits to be used in the education of children in the community. The restitution programme includes profit sharing. This makes it possible to invest back into the business.' [Adapted from https://www.citizen.co.za/news/south-africa/lime-farm-in-hoedspruit]

questions.context: 1.5 Refer to the extract and photograph below on urban blight/decay. URBAN BLIGHT/DECAY IN WYNBERG, CAPE TOWN: 'Over the past decade, business owners have felt helpless as they watched on as the buildings and services in the area have gradually deteriorated. They have tried to get the municipality of Cape Town to take action, but their cries seem to have gone unheard as the issue of urban blight/decay remains unresolved. Leif Petersen, co-director for Sustainable Livelihoods Foundation, whose offices are along the road (shown in the photograph), said that Ebor Road has been in a state of decay for more than a decade. The living conditions in the buildings are terrible - there are illegal water and electricity connections and people sleeping in squalor (filth). "A small, committed group of business owners, including ourselves, have invested time, effort and money in our attempts to implement urban renewal."' questions.context: 2.3 Refer to the infographic below on food security and small/large-scale farming. [FIGURE: Infographic with two photographs on the left - 'Large-scale farming': a tractor spraying long, uniform rows of crops on a vast cultivated field (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/advantages-small-scale-farming); 'Small-scale farming': a group of people cultivating a small plot by hand with hoes.] TEXT PANEL - FOOD SECURITY IN SOUTH AFRICA: 'South Africa has a complex food security situation, with millions of people experiencing food insecurity. In 2024, 25,8% of households faced moderate to severe food insecurity. Both large-scale and small-scale farming are important contributors to food security in South Africa. However, large-scale farmers are often seen as the main drivers of national food security. They can contribute to food security in the region through increased production of agricultural products. Small-scale farmers are important drivers of household food security. The government has implemented programmes to support small-scale farmers, including financial assistance, training and market access. Despite these efforts, food insecurity remains a challenge for many South Africans.' [FIGURE: Horizontal bar graph 'MAJOR CHALLENGES EXPERIENCED BY SMALL- AND LARGE-SCALE FARMERS IN SOUTH AFRICA' (x-axis Percentage 0%-100%; light bars = Large-scale farmers, dark bars = Small-scale farmers): Access to farming equipment/technology - small-scale 19,2 / large-scale 80,8; Access to finance - small-scale 6,9 / large-scale 93,1; Access to arable land - small-scale 25 / large-scale 75.]

questions.context: 2.4 Refer to the extract and map below on the Dube Trade Port Industrial Development Zone (IDZ). DUBE TRADE PORT (IDZ) ATTRACTS INVESTMENTS FROM THE AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY: 'The Dube Trade Port (IDZ) has seen positive economic investments in August 2024 as major automotive (car) companies pledged investment and have set up business in this industrial development zone (IDZ). The automotive industry would join the electronic, high-value manufacturing, food processing and fibre optics sectors at the Dube Trade Port (IDZ). Auto Investment Holdings Group and Mahindra (South Africa) revealed a new assembly plant. Construction of the new assembly plant is expected to be completed in 2025. The company would expand its staff to complement the growing production volumes, as they currently have 90 staff on the assembly line. Ogihara South Africa is a new joint venture between Toyota Tsusho Africa, Ogihara (Thailand) Corporation and Toyota South Africa Motors. They have pledged a R1,2 billion investment among themselves. These companies are building a facility at the Dube Trade Port (IDZ) to manufacture parts for their current and future vehicles.' [Adapted from www.moneyweb] [FIGURE (sciencedirect.com): Satellite-image map of the Durban coast showing DUBE TRANSPORT (Dube Trade Port) in the north, DURBAN HARBOUR 30 km to the south along the OCEAN, TOYOTA SA a further 22 km south, and the Durban-Pinetown Industrial Region inland. Side note: 'The Dube Trade Port (IDZ) is located in the same vicinity as the King Shaka International Airport, 30 minutes from Africa's busiest cargo port, Durban Harbour, and 34 minutes (41 km) from the Durban-Pinetown industrial region.']

questions.context: 2.5 Refer to the infographic below on the informal sector. [FIGURE: Photograph of an informal trader's stall on a pavement with 'Fruit' and 'Vegetables' labelled (bananas, oranges and other produce laid out), captioned "Richard's Bay - informal trader on main road".] TEXT PANEL - GIVE THE INFORMAL SECTOR A BREAK: 'Informal traders are part of the informal sector. Everyone in town has become familiar with the sight of informal traders on the main road in Richards Bay. Most of these informal traders are women without any other income other than selling their goods next to the road. However, during the December holidays, which is normally peak season for informal traders, the municipality fined all of these traders R300 each for selling goods without permits. As it is the only income for some of the informal traders, their income will now take a huge knock. Selling fruit/vegetables/cooked food only twice a week will not cover monthly bills, and some of them are faced with hard times ahead.' [Adapted from https://www.citizen.co.za/zululand-observer/opinion-give-vendors-a-break] TABLE (adapted from https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Busiest-Trading-Months-for-Informal-Traders) - NUMBER OF INFORMAL TRADERS IN RICHARDS BAY CENTRAL BUSINESS DISTRICT (CBD) FOR 2024, MONTH/NUMBER: January 35; February 22; March 38; April 24; May 22; June 42; July 35; August 29; September 46; October 49; November 58; December 60.

questions.context: SECTION B, QUESTION 3: GEOGRAPHICAL SKILLS AND TECHNIQUES. GENERAL INFORMATION ON eMALAHLENI (WITBANK): [FIGURE: outline map of South Africa's provinces with eMALAHLENI marked by a dot in Mpumalanga; north arrow.] Coordinates: 25°50'S; 29°10'E. 'eMalahleni (previously known as Witbank) is a city situated on the Highveld of Mpumalanga, South Africa. eMalahleni is in a coal mining area. Opencast mining is mainly used to extract coal. This type of mining involves digging near the surface to extract coal seams. There are a number of power stations, as well as a steel mill nearby which all require coal. The farmland surrounding eMalahleni is being bought by investors, coal mining companies and real estate developers to accommodate the rapid growth of the city, which is good for local businesses and residents. The region experiences highly polluted air due to the coal mining and power stations.' [Source: https://en.wikipedia.org.Witbank]. English/Afrikaans terms on the topographical map: Cemetery/Begraafplaas; Diggings/Uitgrawings; Golf course/Gholfbaan; Open-cast mine/Oopgroefmyn; River/Rivier; Subsiding ground/Insakkende grond.
